ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
In tank I, whose base has an area of $2 \mathrm{dm}^{2}$ and whose height is $10 \mathrm{~cm}$, the water is $5 \mathrm{~cm}$ high. An empty tank II with a base of area $1 \mathrm{dm}^{2}$ and a height of $7 \mathrm{~cm}$ is placed in tank I. The water of tank I rises, of course, and spills over into tank II. What level does the water reach in tank II?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The diagram shows tank I as an open rectangular tank containing shaded water initially marked at 5 cm high. To the right is an empty open rectangular tank II, marked with height 7 cm, and an arrow indicates tank II is placed into tank I. Reasoning: Convert base areas to square centimeters: tank I has base area 2 dm^2 = 200 cm^2, and tank II has base area 1 dm^2 = 100 cm^2. The initial water volume in tank I is 200 × 5 = 1000 cm^3. When tank II is placed in tank I and the water outside reaches the rim of tank II, the outside water level is 7 cm. Since tank II occupies 100 cm^2 of the base area, the water outside tank II occupies the remaining base area 200 − 100 = 100 cm^2. Thus the outside water volume is 100 × 7 = 700 cm^3. The remaining water volume is 1000 − 700 = 300 cm^3, which spills into tank II. Tank II has base area 100 cm^2, so the water height inside it is 300 ÷ 100 = 3 cm.

When tank II sits inside tank I and water has just spilled over its rim, the outside water level in tank I is at the 7 cm rim of tank II. The remaining water volume is 1000 − 700 = 300 cm^3, and this is inside tank II. Since tank II’s base area is 100 cm^2, the water height inside it is 300 ÷ 100 = 3 cm.

method.method_draft: First read the diagram: the shaded water in tank I is initially 5 cm high, tank II is an open rectangular vessel 7 cm tall, and the arrow shows it being inserted into tank I. From the text, the initial water volume is 2 dm^2 × 5 cm = 2 dm^2 × 0.5 dm = 1 dm^3. After tank II is placed in tank I, the area available for water outside tank II is 2 dm^2 − 1 dm^2 = 1 dm^2. If no water could enter tank II, this 1 dm^3 of water would stand outside tank II to height 1 dm^3 ÷ 1 dm^2 = 1 dm = 10 cm. But tank II is only 7 cm tall, so the hypothetical outside column exceeds the rim by 10 − 7 = 3 cm. That excess water must spill over into tank II. Because the excess volume is a 3 cm column over area 1 dm^2, and tank II also has base area 1 dm^2, the water level inside tank II becomes 3 cm.
